mcq.q: 1 parsec equals approximately
mcq.exp: 1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light years ≈ 3.08×10¹⁶ m.

mcq.q: 1 fermi equals
mcq.exp: 1 fermi = 1 femtometre = 10⁻¹⁵ m; used for nuclear size.

mcq.q: The least count of a vernier caliper with 10 VSD = 9 MSD is
mcq.exp: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm.

mcq.q: Order of magnitude of 4700 is
mcq.exp: 4700 ≈ 5×10³; since 5 > √10, order of magnitude = 10⁴ ... actually 4700 rounds to 10³·⁶⁷ → order = 10⁴. But conventionally 4700 ~ 10³. Wait: order of magnitude = nearest power of 10. log₁₀(4700)=3.67, nearest integer = 4. So 10⁴.

mcq.q: In a screw gauge, if the pitch is 0.5 mm and number of circular scale divisions is 50, the least count is
mcq.exp: LC = pitch/number of CSD = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.

vsa.q: What is the least count of an instrument?
vsa.ans: The least count is the smallest value that can be measured or read directly with the instrument.
1 parsec = 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.26 light years. It is the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond.

sa1.q: A student measures diameter of a sphere as 2.4 cm with a vernier caliper (LC = 0.01 cm). Find volume with proper significant figures and error.
Explain parallax method for measuring large distances.
sa1.ans:
In parallax, the apparent shift in position of a distant object when viewed from two different positions is measured.
For celestial bodies: baseline b (distance between two observation points on Earth) and parallax angle θ are measured.
Distance D = b / (2 sin(θ/2)) ≈ b/θ for small angles.
Used to measure distances to nearby stars.

la.q: Describe various measuring instruments used in a physics laboratory and their applications.

parts.q: Explain the construction and working of a vernier caliper. How do you take a reading?
parts.ans:
A vernier caliper has two jaws — one fixed on the main scale (MS) and one sliding with a vernier scale (VS). The vernier scale has n divisions = (n-1) main scale divisions.
Reading: (i) Note main scale reading just before the zero of vernier (MS reading). (ii) Find the vernier division that coincides with a main scale division (VS reading). (iii) Total reading = MS reading + (VS reading × LC). LC = 1 MSD/n for n VS divisions.

parts.q: What is a screw gauge? Define its pitch and least count. A screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular scale divisions — find its least count and range of error.
parts.ans: Screw gauge: measures small thickness/diameter using screw principle. Pitch = advance per revolution = 0.5 mm. LC = Pitch/No. of CSD = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. Error range = ± LC/2 = ± 0.005 mm.

mcq.q: A river 100 m wide flows at 3 m/s. A boat can row at 5 m/s in still water. Minimum time to cross is
mcq.exp: Min time: row perpendicular to banks. t = 100/5 = 20 s.

sa2.q: A river is 200 m wide and flows at 4 m/s. A boat rows at 5 m/s relative to water. (i) In what direction should boat row to go straight across? (ii) Time taken. (iii) What is minimum time to cross?
sa2.ans:
(i) Let boat angle θ upstream. Net vₓ=0: 5sinθ=4 → θ=sin⁻¹(0.8)≈53° upstream.
vy=5cosθ=5×0.6=3 m/s.
(ii) t=200/3=66.7 s.
(iii) Min time: row perpendicular. t=200/5=40 s (drifts 4×40=160 m downstream).

la.q: Discuss circular motion, centripetal acceleration, and banking of roads.

parts.q: Derive centripetal acceleration in circular motion. Show why a body moving in a circle must have a net inward force.
parts.ans:
Position: r = r cosωt î + r sinωt ĵ.
Velocity: v = −rω sinωt î + rω cosωt ĵ; |v| = rω = constant.
Acceleration: a = −rω² cosωt î − rω² sinωt ĵ = −ω²r.
Magnitude: ω²r = v²/r; direction: opposite to r = toward center.
For this acceleration, net force F = mv²/r must act toward center (centripetal force).

parts.q: A 500 kg car moves at 10 m/s on a circular track of radius 50 m. What friction force is needed? If μ = 0.3, is this safe? (g=10)

la.q: Explain relative velocity in two dimensions with applications.

parts.q: Define relative velocity in 2D. If A moves at vₐ and B at v_B, write the expression and explain geometrically. Apply to rain problem.
parts.ans:
v_AB = v_A − v_B (vector subtraction).
Geometrically: draw v_A and −v_B head to tail; resultant = v_AB.
Rain problem: rain falls at v_r vertically. Person walks at v_p horizontally. Relative velocity of rain w.r.t. person = v_r − v_p. Person must tilt umbrella at angle θ = arctan(v_p/v_r) forward.

parts.q: A boat goes 30 km upstream in 3 h and returns in 1.5 h. Find speed of boat in still water and river current.
parts.ans:
Let boat speed = v_b, current = v_c.
Upstream: (v_b − v_c) = 30/3 = 10 km/h.
Downstream: (v_b + v_c) = 30/1.5 = 20 km/h.
v_b = 15 km/h; v_c = 5 km/h.

mcq.q: Pseudo force arises in
mcq.exp: In a non-inertial (accelerating) frame, a pseudo force (= −ma_frame) is added.

mcq.q: Body on incline: angle of repose θ₀ satisfies
mcq.exp: At angle of repose: mg sinθ₀ = μmg cosθ₀ → tanθ₀ = μ.

la.q: Discuss laws of friction, angle of friction, and angle of repose.

parts.q: State laws of friction and explain angle of friction. Derive relationship between angle of friction and coefficient of friction.
parts.ans:
Laws: (1) f ≤ μN; (2) independent of area; (3) f_k independent of speed.
Angle of friction λ: angle between resultant reaction and normal. tanλ = f/N = μN/N = μ → λ = arctan(μ).
For incline, angle of repose θ₀ = λ, because at θ₀ the body is about to slide: tanθ₀ = μ.

parts.q: A 10 kg block on incline (θ=45°) with μₛ=0.5, μₖ=0.4. Does it slide? If yes, find acceleration. (g=10)

mcq.q: Coefficient of restitution for perfectly elastic collision is:
mcq.exp: For perfectly elastic collision, e = 1 (relative speed of separation = relative speed of approach).

vsa.ans: Coefficient of restitution e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach). For elastic collision e=1, perfectly inelastic e=0.

mcq.q: Rolling without slipping requires:
mcq.exp: For rolling without slipping, the contact point velocity = 0. This gives v_cm = ωR.

mcq.q: Parallel axis theorem states: I = I_cm + ?
mcq.exp: Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md² where d is distance between the two parallel axes.

mcq.q: For a rolling body, ratio of translational KE to rotational KE for solid sphere is:
mcq.exp: For solid sphere: I=2MR²/5. KE_trans/KE_rot = (½Mv²)/(½Iω²) = Mv²/(Iω²) = MR²/(2MR²/5) = 5/2.

mcq.q: Perpendicular axis theorem applies to:
mcq.exp: Perpendicular axis theorem (Iz = Ix + Iy) applies only to laminar (flat, 2D) bodies.

mcq.q: For a rolling body on inclined plane, acceleration is:
mcq.exp: Rolling on incline: a = g sinθ/(1 + I/MR²). Smaller I → greater acceleration.

vsa.ans: For a lamina in XY plane, Iz = Ix + Iy, where Iz, Ix, Iy are moments of inertia about Z, X, Y axes respectively.
Moment of inertia about any axis = moment of inertia about parallel axis through CM + Md², where d = distance between axes.

sa1.q: Derive expression for KE of a rolling body (without slipping).
sa1.ans:
A rolling body has both translational and rotational motion.

Translational KE = ½Mv_cm²
Rotational KE = ½Iω²

For rolling without slipping: v_cm = ωR → ω = v_cm/R

Total KE = ½Mv_cm² + ½I(v_cm/R)²
= ½Mv_cm²(1 + I/MR²)
= ½Mv_cm²(1 + K²/R²)

where K = radius of gyration.

sa2.q: Derive an expression for moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod about an axis through its center, perpendicular to its length.
sa2.ans:
Rod of mass M, length L. Consider element at distance x from center, width dx.

Mass per unit length = M/L
Mass of element dm = (M/L)dx

Moment of inertia of element: dI = x²dm = x²(M/L)dx

I = ∫dI from −L/2 to L/2
= (M/L)∫x²dx from −L/2 to +L/2
= (M/L)[x³/3] from −L/2 to L/2
= (M/L) × (2/3)(L/2)³
= (M/L) × (L³/12)
= ML²/12

la.q: Explain the concept of moment of inertia. Derive the expression for a solid cylinder about its axis. State and prove theorems of MI.

parts.q: Define MI and derive for solid cylinder about axis.
parts.ans:
Moment of Inertia (MI): Rotational analog of mass; measures resistance to rotational acceleration.
I = Σmᵢrᵢ² (discrete) or I = ∫r²dm (continuous)

Solid Cylinder about axis:
Consider thin cylindrical shell of radius r, thickness dr, length L, density ρ.

Volume of shell = 2πrL dr
dm = ρ × 2πrL dr = (M/πR²L) × 2πrL dr = 2Mr dr/R²

dI = r² dm = r² × (2Mr/R²)dr = 2Mr³/R² dr

I = ∫dI from 0 to R = (2M/R²) ∫r³ dr from 0 to R
= (2M/R²) × R⁴/4 = MR²/2

I_solid cylinder = ½MR²

parts.q: Parallel axis and perpendicular axis theorems.
parts.ans:
1. Parallel Axis Theorem (all bodies):
I = I_cm + Md²
where d = perpendicular distance between parallel axis and axis through CM.
Proof sketch: I = Σmᵢrᵢ² for any axis; expand rᵢ² using distance from CM → get I_cm + Md².

Example: Rod about end = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + ML²/4 = ML²/3

2. Perpendicular Axis Theorem (laminar bodies only):
Iz = Ix + Iy
Z is perpendicular to lamina; X, Y are in the plane.
Proof: For particle at (x,y): Iz contribution = m(x²+y²) = mx² + my² = Iy contribution + Ix contribution. Sum over all particles.

num.q: A solid cylinder rolls down an incline of height 1 m. Find speed at bottom. (g=10 m/s²)
num.ans:
For rolling cylinder: ½Mv²(1 + ½) = Mgh
¾v² = 10 × 1
v² = 40/3
v = √(13.33) = 3.65 m/s

mcq.q: For a geostationary satellite, its time period must be:
mcq.exp: Geostationary satellite has time period equal to Earth's rotation period = 24 hours.

mcq.q: Weightlessness in a satellite is due to:
opts: Satellite being very far from Earth
Both satellite and astronaut in free fall
mcq.exp: In orbit, both satellite and everything inside are in free fall (centripetal = gravitational). Normal force = 0 → apparent weightlessness.

mcq.q: Gravitational field is:
opts: Vector quantity directed toward the mass
Vector quantity directed away from mass
mcq.exp: Gravitational field g = F/m, directed toward the source mass (attractive). It is a vector.

vsa.q: What is a geostationary satellite? Where is it placed?
vsa.ans: Satellite with time period 24 hours, orbiting in equatorial plane from west to east. Appears stationary relative to Earth. Placed at ≈36,000 km above equator.

la.q: Describe Newton's law of gravitation. Explain how Kepler's laws can be derived from it. Discuss the concept of gravitational field and potential.

parts.q: Newton's law and deriving Kepler's third law.
parts.ans:
Newton's Law of Gravitation:
Every body attracts every other body with force: F = Gm₁m₂/r²

Properties:
1. Always attractive
2. Acts along line joining masses
3. Central force (radial)
4. Long range — extends to infinity
5. Obeys Newton's 3rd law

G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻²

Deriving Kepler's 3rd Law (circular orbit):
For planet of mass m orbiting Sun (mass M) in circle of radius r:
Gravitational force = centripetal force
GMm/r² = mω²r
GM = ω²r³
GM = (2π/T)²r³
T² = (4π²/GM)r³
T² ∝ r³ — Kepler's third law proved!

parts.q: Gravitational field and gravitational potential.
parts.ans:
Gravitational Field (g):
The gravitational field at a point is the force per unit mass:
g = F/m = GM/r² (directed toward mass M)
Field is a vector quantity.
Field lines go radially inward toward mass.

Gravitational Potential (V):
Work done per unit mass to bring test mass from infinity:
V = W/m = −GM/r (negative — attractive)

Relation: g = −dV/dr

Potential is scalar. Equipotential surfaces are spheres around M.
The potential well concept: masses create 'dips' in space-time (general relativity analogy).

la.q: Explain geostationary satellites. Derive the height of geostationary orbit. Discuss applications.

parts.q: Derive height of geostationary orbit.
parts.ans:
Geostationary Satellite:
Time period T = 24 h = 86400 s
Orbits in equatorial plane, west to east
Appears stationary to ground observers

Derivation of height:
From orbital mechanics:
T = 2π(R+h)^(3/2)/√(GM)

T² = 4π²(R+h)³/GM
(R+h)³ = GMT²/4π²

Using G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹, M = 6×10²⁴ kg, T = 86400 s:
GMT² = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 6×10²⁴ × (86400)²
= 4×10¹⁴ × 7.46×10⁹ = 2.98×10²⁴

(R+h)³ = 2.98×10²⁴/39.48 = 7.54×10²²
R+h = (7.54×10²²)^(1/3) = 4.22×10⁷ m
h = 4.22×10⁷ − 6.4×10⁶ ≈ 3.6×10⁷ m = 36,000 km

parts.q: Applications of geostationary satellites.
parts.ans:
Applications:

1. Telecommunications: Relay voice, data, TV signals globally. INSAT series.
2. Weather forecasting: METEOSAT, INSAT-3D observe cloud patterns, storms.
3. GPS navigation: Though GPS uses MEO satellites, same orbital mechanics.
4. Broadcasting: Direct-to-home (DTH) TV services.
5. Remote sensing: Monitor agricultural land, forest cover, disasters.
6. Internet: Satellite internet coverage for remote areas.

Limitations:
- 36,000 km distance causes signal delay (~0.5 s round trip)
- Large rocket needed to launch to such height
- Only ~180 geostationary slots available above equator

sa2.q: Define bulk modulus. Derive the expression. What is compressibility? Calculate compressibility of water if bulk modulus is 2.2×10⁹ Pa.
sa2.ans:
Bulk Modulus:
When a body is subjected to uniform pressure P (all sides), it experiences volumetric stress = P and volumetric strain = −ΔV/V.

Bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V) = −PV/ΔV

(Negative sign: P increases → V decreases; makes B positive)

Compressibility = 1/B (ease of compression)

For water: B = 2.2×10⁹ Pa
Compressibility = 1/(2.2×10⁹) = 4.55×10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹

Water is very incompressible — small compressibility.

mcq.q: For laminar flow, Reynolds number is:
mcq.exp: Laminar flow: Re < 1000 (approximately). Turbulent flow: Re > 4000. Transition: 1000-4000.

mcq.q: Newton's law of cooling states that rate of heat loss is proportional to:
opts: Temperature difference between body and surroundings
mcq.exp: Newton's law: dQ/dt ∝ (T − T_s) where T = body temperature, T_s = surrounding temperature.

mcq.q: The peak wavelength of radiation from a blackbody is related to its temperature T by:
mcq.exp: Wien's displacement law: λ_max × T = constant = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K. λ_max ∝ 1/T.

mcq.q: During regelation, ice melts under:
opts: High pressure and refreezes on removal of pressure
mcq.exp: Regelation: Ice melts under pressure (pressure lowers melting point) and refreezes when pressure is removed. Enables ice skating.

vsa.ans: The rate of heat loss of a body is proportional to the difference between the temperature of the body and its surroundings: dQ/dt ∝ (T − T_s).

vsa.q: What is Kirchhoff's law of radiation?
vsa.ans: At any temperature, the ratio of emissive power to absorptive power is the same for all bodies and equals the emissive power of a perfect black body: e/a = E_b.

la.q: Explain heat transfer by conduction and radiation. Derive Fourier's law. Discuss good and bad conductors with applications.

parts.q: Conduction: Fourier's law, good/bad conductors.
parts.ans:
Conduction:
Heat transfer through vibrations passed from atom to atom, without bulk movement.

Fourier's Law:
Heat flow rate: H = dQ/dt = −KA(dT/dx)
Where: K = thermal conductivity, A = cross-section area, dT/dx = temperature gradient

For slab: H = KA(T₁−T₂)/L

Thermal conductivity K:
• Metals: high K (copper 385 W/m·K, iron 80 W/m·K)
• Non-metals: low K (wood ~0.1, glass ~1)
• Gases: very low K (air ~0.026)

Good conductors: metals (free electrons carry heat)
Bad conductors (insulators): wool, wood, glass, air

Applications:
• Copper bottomed cooking vessels: fast heat transfer
• Wooden handles on metal tools: low K for safety
• Igloo: air trapped in snow acts as insulator
• Thermos flask: vacuum between walls prevents conduction

parts.q: Radiation: Stefan law, Wien's law, greenhouse effect.
parts.ans:
Radiation:
Heat transfer via electromagnetic waves. Requires no medium.

Perfect black body: absorbs all radiation. ε = 1.
Emissive power: E = σT⁴ (Stefan law)

Wien's Law: λ_max T = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K

For real bodies: E = εσT⁴ (ε = emissivity, 0 to 1)

Newton's Law of Cooling (approximate):
dT/dt = −k(T − T_s) for small temperature differences
T(t) = T_s + (T₀ − T_s)e^(−kt)

Greenhouse Effect:
Sun (high T, ~5800 K): emits mostly visible light (short λ)
Earth surface: absorbs, warms up, emits IR (long λ)
CO₂, H₂O, CH₄: transparent to visible, opaque to IR
Thermal energy trapped → Earth warms
Enhanced greenhouse effect due to human emissions → climate change

num.q: Sun's surface temp is 5800 K. Find peak wavelength. (Wien's constant b = 2.9×10⁻³ m·K)

mcq.q: The efficiency of Carnot engine operating between temperatures T₁ (source) and T₂ (sink) is:
mcq.exp: Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ where T₁ = source temperature, T₂ = sink temperature (in Kelvin).

mcq.q: The Carnot cycle consists of:
opts: Two isothermal and two adiabatic processes
mcq.exp: Carnot cycle: isothermal expansion → adiabatic expansion → isothermal compression → adiabatic compression.

mcq.q: Entropy is a measure of:
mcq.exp: Entropy S measures the disorder or randomness of a system. ΔS = Q/T for reversible process.

mcq.q: A refrigerator is a heat engine working in:
mcq.exp: Refrigerator works as a reversed heat engine: uses work to transfer heat from cold to hot reservoir.

mcq.q: COP (coefficient of performance) of a refrigerator is:
opts: Heat absorbed from cold reservoir/Work input
mcq.exp: COP = Q₂/W = Q₂/(Q₁−Q₂) where Q₂ = heat from cold body, W = work input.

mcq.q: A Carnot engine has efficiency 50%. If sink temperature is 300 K, source temperature is:

vsa.q: Define the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator.
vsa.ans: COP = Q₂/W = heat absorbed from cold reservoir / work input. Higher COP means more efficient refrigerator.

vsa.q: Why is Carnot engine called a reversible engine?
vsa.ans: Carnot engine uses only reversible processes (isothermal and adiabatic) — no friction, no sudden changes. It can run forwards or backwards without entropy generation.

vsa.q: What is entropy? What happens to entropy in a spontaneous process?
vsa.ans: Entropy S = measure of disorder of a system. ΔS = Qrev/T. In any spontaneous irreversible process, total entropy of universe increases.

vsa.q: How does a heat pump differ from a refrigerator?
vsa.ans: Both work on same principle (reversed Carnot). Refrigerator: cool the cold body (goal = remove heat from cold). Heat pump: warm the hot body (goal = add heat to hot space).

sa1.q: A Carnot engine works between 600 K and 300 K. Find efficiency and heat rejected if heat absorbed = 1000 J.
sa1.ans:
Efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 − 300/600 = 0.5 = 50%

Work done W = ηQ₁ = 0.5 × 1000 = 500 J

Heat rejected Q₂ = Q₁ − W = 1000 − 500 = 500 J

Or: Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁ → Q₂ = 1000 × 300/600 = 500 J

sa1.q: Describe the four processes of a Carnot cycle.
sa1.ans:
1. Isothermal expansion (A→B): Gas absorbs Q₁ from hot reservoir at T₁; expands isothermally.

2. Adiabatic expansion (B→C): Gas expands adiabatically; temperature falls from T₁ to T₂.

3. Isothermal compression (C→D): Gas rejects Q₂ to cold reservoir at T₂; compressed isothermally.

4. Adiabatic compression (D→A): Gas compressed adiabatically; temperature rises from T₂ back to T₁.

Net work = Q₁ − Q₂. Efficiency = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁.

sa2.q: Derive expression for efficiency of Carnot engine. Show it is maximum for reversible engines.
sa2.ans:
Carnot cycle: Absorbs Q₁ from source T₁, rejects Q₂ to sink T₂.

For reversible isothermal expansion (A→B):
Q₁ = nRT₁ ln(V_B/V_A)

For reversible isothermal compression (C→D):
Q₂ = nRT₂ ln(V_C/V_D)

For adiabatic processes:
T₁V_B^(γ-1) = T₂V_C^(γ-1)  ...(adiabatic B→C)
T₁V_A^(γ-1) = T₂V_D^(γ-1)  ...(adiabatic D→A)
Divide: (V_B/V_A) = (V_C/V_D)

Therefore: Q₁/Q₂ = T₁/T₂

Efficiency: η = W/Q₁ = (Q₁−Q₂)/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁

Carnot's theorem: All reversible engines between same temperatures have same efficiency. Irreversible engines have lower efficiency.
η_irreversible < η_Carnot = 1 − T₂/T₁

sa2.q: What is a heat pump? Derive its COP. Compare COP of heat pump and refrigerator.
sa2.ans:
Heat Pump:
Device that extracts heat from cold body and delivers it to hot body using work.
Use: Space heating (takes heat from cold outside, delivers to warm inside).

COP of Heat Pump (heating effect):
COP_HP = Q₁/W
Where Q₁ = heat delivered to hot reservoir, W = work input.

Since Q₁ = Q₂ + W:
COP_HP = Q₁/W = (Q₂+W)/W = 1 + Q₂/W = 1 + COP_refrigerator

For Carnot heat pump:
COP_HP = T₁/(T₁−T₂) = 1/(1−T₂/T₁)

COP_refrigerator = Q₂/W = T₂/(T₁−T₂)

COP_HP = COP_ref + 1 > COP_ref always.

For T₁=300K, T₂=273K:
COP_HP = 300/27 ≈ 11 (delivers 11 J for every 1 J work)
Very efficient space heating!

la.q: Explain the laws of thermodynamics. Derive the efficiency of a Carnot engine. Discuss why 100% efficiency is impossible.

parts.q: First law and Carnot efficiency derivation.
parts.ans:
First Law: ΔU = Q − W

For a cycle: ΔU = 0, so Q_net = W_net (cyclic process)

Carnot Engine Efficiency:
Carnot cycle uses: isothermal expansion at T₁ (absorbs Q₁), adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression at T₂ (rejects Q₂), adiabatic compression.

For reversible isothermal processes:
Q₁ = nRT₁ ln(V_B/V_A)
Q₂ = nRT₂ ln(V_C/V_D)

From adiabatic processes: V_B/V_A = V_C/V_D

Therefore: Q₁/Q₂ = T₁/T₂

Efficiency: η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁

For T₁=500K, T₂=300K: η = 1−300/500 = 40%

parts.q: Why 100% efficiency is impossible, and significance of 2nd law.
parts.ans:
Why 100% efficiency is impossible:
1. Kelvin-Planck statement: Cannot convert all heat to work.
2. For 100% efficiency: T₂ = 0 K (sink at absolute zero) — unachievable.
3. Or T₁ = ∞ — also unachievable.

Practical engines always have:
• Friction losses
• Heat losses
• Non-reversible processes
• Real efficiency << Carnot efficiency

Significance of 2nd Law:
• Defines arrow of time (events go one way)
• Spontaneous processes increase entropy
• Universe tends toward disorder
• Limits efficiency of ALL engines, not just heat engines
• Explains why evolution of universe goes toward disorder (heat death)

num.q: Carnot engine: T₁=500K, T₂=300K. Efficiency and work done if Q₁=1000J.
COP of refrigerator operating between 260K (cold) and 300K (hot).
num.ans:
COP = T₂/(T₁−T₂) = 260/(300−260) = 260/40 = 6.5
For each 1 J of work, 6.5 J of heat removed from cold reservoir.

num.q: Carnot engine efficiency 30%. Sink at 280K. Find source temperature.

sa2.q: State and prove the law of equipartition of energy. Use it to find specific heats of monatomic and diatomic gases.
sa2.ans:
Equipartition Theorem:
'In thermal equilibrium, each quadratic term in the energy expression (each degree of freedom) has average energy (1/2)kT.'

For a monatomic gas (f = 3 translational DOF):
E = ½mv_x² + ½mv_y² + ½mv_z²
Average energy per molecule = 3 × (1/2)kT = (3/2)kT

For n moles: U = n × N_A × (3/2)kT = (3/2)nRT
Cv = (1/n)(dU/dT) = (3/2)R = 12.5 J/mol·K
Cp = Cv + R = (5/2)R = 20.8 J/mol·K
γ = 5/3 = 1.67

For diatomic gas (f = 5; 3 trans + 2 rot at room temp):
U = (5/2)nRT
Cv = (5/2)R = 20.8 J/mol·K
Cp = (7/2)R = 29.1 J/mol·K
γ = 7/5 = 1.4

sa2.q: Derive expressions for mean speed, rms speed, and most probable speed. Compare them.
sa2.ans:
For Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution:

1. Most Probable Speed (v_mp):
At peak of distribution, df/dv = 0:
v_mp = √(2RT/M) = √(2kT/m)

2. Mean Speed (v_mean):
v_mean = √(8RT/πM) = √(8kT/πm)

3. RMS Speed:
v_rms = √(3RT/M) = √(3kT/m)

Comparison:
v_mp : v_mean : v_rms = √2 : √(8/π) : √3
= 1 : 1.128 : 1.225
= 1.000 : 1.128 : 1.225

v_mp < v_mean < v_rms

For N₂ at 300K:
v_mp = 422 m/s
v_mean = 476 m/s
v_rms = 517 m/s

la.q: Discuss the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution. Explain the concept of mean free path and its significance.

parts.q: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and three speeds.
parts.ans:
Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution:
f(v) = 4π(m/2πkT)^(3/2) × v² × e^(-mv²/2kT)

Features:
• f(0) = 0 (no molecules at rest)
• f → 0 as v → ∞ (few very fast molecules)
• Peak at most probable speed v_mp
• Asymmetric — tail on high-speed side

With increasing temperature:
• Distribution flattens and shifts right
• v_mp, v_mean, v_rms all increase
• More molecules in high-speed tail

Three characteristic speeds:
v_mp = √(2RT/M) ← at peak
v_mean = √(8RT/πM) ← arithmetic mean
v_rms = √(3RT/M) ← √(mean of v²)

v_mp < v_mean < v_rms

For H₂ at 300K:
v_mp ≈ 1580 m/s, v_rms ≈ 1934 m/s

parts.q: Mean free path and its significance.
parts.ans:
Mean Free Path (λ):
λ = 1/(√2nπd²) = kT/(√2πd²P)

Typical values: ~10⁻⁷ m at STP for N₂

Significance:
1. Determines transport properties (viscosity, thermal conductivity, diffusion)
2. λ >> atomic spacing → gas molecules mostly free
3. If λ << dimensions of container: classical gas behavior
4. If λ ≈ container dimensions: Knudsen flow (vacuum tubes)

Related concepts:
• Viscosity: η ∝ λρv_mean (momentum transport)
• Thermal conductivity: K ∝ λρv_mean Cv
• Diffusion: D ∝ λv_mean

Applications:
• Design of vacuum systems
• Understanding atmospheric phenomena
• Plasma physics and fusion research

mcq.q: Resonance occurs when applied frequency equals:
mcq.exp: Resonance: When driving frequency = natural frequency, amplitude becomes maximum.

mcq.q: Two springs k₁ and k₂ are in parallel. Effective k is:
mcq.exp: Springs in parallel: k_eff = k₁ + k₂.

mcq.q: Forced oscillation is:
opts: Oscillation driven by external periodic force
mcq.exp: Forced oscillation: system oscillates at driving frequency (not its own natural frequency) due to an external periodic force.

vsa.ans: Resonance occurs when the frequency of the external driving force equals the natural frequency of the oscillating system. Amplitude becomes maximum.

vsa.q: What is damped oscillation? Give one example.
vsa.ans: Damped oscillation: amplitude decreases with time due to energy loss from friction/resistance. Example: oscillating pendulum in air; LC circuit with resistance.

sa2.q: Explain free, forced and resonant oscillations with examples. Distinguish between them.
sa2.ans:
1. Free (Natural) Oscillation:
• System oscillates at its natural frequency f₀
• No external driving force
• If undamped: amplitude constant
• Example: pendulum disturbed and left to swing; vibrating tuning fork in absence of friction

2. Forced (Driven) Oscillation:
• External periodic force applied at frequency f
• System oscillates at driving frequency f (not f₀)
• If f ≠ f₀: amplitude is small
• Energy continuously supplied by driver
• Example: child being pushed on swing at regular intervals

3. Resonance:
• Special case of forced oscillation when f = f₀
• Amplitude becomes very large
• Energy transfer is most efficient
• Destructive if structure resonates with earthquake/wind
• Examples: Tacoma Narrows bridge collapse; soldiers breaking step on bridges; radio tuning (electrical resonance)

Key difference: free uses f₀; forced uses external f; resonance when both are equal.

sa2.q: Two springs of constants 3 N/m and 6 N/m are connected in series supporting 1 kg. Find: (a) effective spring constant (b) time period (c) energy if amplitude is 0.05 m.

la.q: Explain superposition principle, beats and resonance. Discuss applications of resonance.

parts.q: Superposition and resonance.
parts.ans:
Principle of Superposition:
When multiple waves/oscillations overlap, resultant displacement = vector sum of individual displacements.

For two SHM of same frequency and amplitude but different phase:
x₁ = A sinωt, x₂ = A sin(ωt + φ)
x = x₁ + x₂ = 2A cos(φ/2) sin(ωt + φ/2)
Resultant amplitude = 2A cos(φ/2)

Resonance:
Every system has natural frequency f₀.
When external driving frequency = f₀:
• Amplitude builds up to very large value
• Energy transfer is maximum
• System absorbs energy most efficiently

Mathematical: For driven SHM: A = F₀/(m√((ω₀²−ω²)²+4β²ω²))
At ω = ω₀ (undamped): A → ∞
With damping: A = F₀/(2mβω₀) (finite but large)

parts.q: Applications and dangers of resonance.
parts.ans:
Beneficial Applications:
1. Radio/TV tuning: LC circuit resonates at broadcast frequency
2. MRI (NMR): nuclear magnetic resonance for medical imaging
3. Microwave oven: water molecules resonate at microwave frequency
4. Musical instruments: resonating air columns (flute, organ pipes)
5. Quartz watches: piezoelectric crystal oscillates at precise frequency

Dangerous Resonance:
1. Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940): Wind vortices matched bridge's natural frequency → collapse
2. Soldiers 'break step' on bridges to avoid resonance
3. Earthquakes: buildings with natural frequency matching seismic frequency suffer most damage
4. Aeroplane wing flutter: wings must avoid resonance with engine frequency

Damping: Added to structures to reduce resonance amplitude (shock absorbers, vibration isolators).

mcq.q: The Doppler effect refers to:
opts: Change in amplitude due to motion
Change in frequency due to relative motion of source/observer
mcq.exp: Doppler effect: observed frequency changes when source or observer are in relative motion.

mcq.q: Reverberation is due to:
mcq.exp: Reverberation: persistence of sound after source stops, due to multiple reflections from walls/ceiling/floor.

vsa.q: What is Doppler effect? Give one application.
vsa.ans: Change in observed frequency due to relative motion between source and observer. Application: Police radar (measuring speed), medical Doppler ultrasound.

sa1.q: State Doppler's effect. A police car siren (1200 Hz) moves at 30 m/s toward a wall. Find frequency heard by observer behind the car. (v_sound = 330 m/s)
sa1.ans:
Doppler formula when source moves toward wall and observer is behind:

For the wall (acting as observer, source moving toward it):
f_wall = f₀ × v/(v − vs) = 1200 × 330/(330−30) = 1200 × 330/300 = 1320 Hz

The wall reflects 1320 Hz back. Now wall is source, observer (behind car) is stationary, car (source) moves away from wall:
f_observer = f_reflected × v/(v + vs) = 1320 × 330/360 = 1210 Hz

(Simple case if observer is stationary in front: f = 1200 × 330/300 = 1320 Hz)

sa2.q: Derive the Doppler effect formula for all cases of motion of source and observer.
sa2.ans:
Let source emit frequency f₀. Speed of sound = v.

Case 1: Source moving toward stationary observer at speed vs:
Effective wavelength: λ' = (v − vs)/f₀
Observed: f = v/λ' = vf₀/(v − vs)

Case 2: Source moving away at vs:
λ' = (v + vs)/f₀
f = vf₀/(v + vs)

Case 3: Observer moving toward stationary source at v₀:
Relative speed of waves = v + v₀
f = (v + v₀)f₀/v

Case 4: Observer moving away at v₀:
f = (v − v₀)f₀/v

General formula:
f = f₀ × (v + v₀)/(v + vs)
(Signs: + for motion toward, − for motion away)

Applications: Radar speed guns, medical ultrasound, astronomical redshift.
